transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi. Thank you. Um, well, I'm here because I just... I really need some help with how much I'm obsessing over my face. It's specifically the left side of my face. I just can't stop focusing on how uneven and, like, puffy it looks. 

I work as a computer support specialist, so I am constantly, and I mean constantly, on video calls all day long for my job. And the whole time I'm supposed to be helping someone fix their network or whatever, I'm just staring at my own little video square on the screen, looking at how swollen and lopsided my left cheek and jaw area are. It's exhausting. And it's bleeding into my personal life, too. I love salsa dancing, it's kind of my main social outlet, but whenever people take photos at the socials—which they do all the time for Instagram and stuff—I just look at them afterward and the puffiness is so incredibly obvious to me. 

But the crazy part, and the reason I guess I'm sitting here, is that everyone keeps telling me they don't see anything. My friends, my dance partners, they all swear my face is completely normal and they don't know what I'm talking about. But I know what I see. And it's really starting to mess with my work and my social life, because I'm constantly trying to angle my camera at work to hide that side of my face, and I'm starting to skip dance nights altogether just to avoid the photos. I just can't stop thinking about it, and it's taking over everything.

Can you tell me how certain you are that the left side of your face is actually swollen and uneven? Have you considered that it might just be how your face naturally looks, even though others don’t see it the way you do?

I mean... I am... I'm very certain of what I see. I really am. It’s hard because, like I was saying, everyone tells me I’m just seeing things. But when I look in the mirror, or when I'm staring at that little webcam feed on my monitor, it is just... it’s right there. It’s not some subtle, barely-there thing to me. 

I know people say, "Oh, nobody's face is perfectly symmetrical," and I get that. I went to grad school, I'm a logical person, I understand that human faces have natural variations and one eye is usually slightly bigger than the other or whatever. But this isn't just a normal, everyday variation. It literally looks like... you know when you have a dental procedure, like a root canal or getting a wisdom tooth out, and your cheek gets all puffy and swollen? It looks like the tail end of that. Like there's this permanent, heavy pocket of swelling just sitting right there along my left jawline and cheek. 

And I really do try to tell myself what you're saying, you know? I try to rationalize it. I'll say, "Maybe this is just how I look, maybe this is just my face and I need to accept it." I'll literally stand in my bathroom—because the lighting in there is really harsh, it’s those bright overhead vanity bulbs—and I’ll try to force myself to see what my friends see. I'll tell myself it's completely normal. But then I'll turn my head even a fraction of an inch, or the light will catch the side of my cheek, and the shadow it creates just highlights the unevenness so perfectly. And then I'm just stuck there. I'll spend I don't even know how long just analyzing the curve of it, comparing the left side to the right side, sometimes using my hand to cover one side of my face and then the other, or pulling my skin back a little just to see what it *should* look like if it were normal. 

So... I guess I've tried to consider that it’s just my natural face, mostly because I feel like I have to based on what everyone else says. But in the moment? When I'm actually looking at it? I am completely, completely certain that it is swollen and lopsided. It's just so real to me. I can't unsee it, no matter how hard I try to convince myself otherwise.

Have you ever questioned whether your belief about the left side of your face being swollen might not be accurate, even for a moment, or does it feel absolutely certain to you no matter how much you or others try to reason about it?

I mean... I guess there are these tiny, tiny fractions of a second where I think, 'Okay, maybe they're right.' Like, if my best friend—who I've known since grad school, she's practically my sister and she would absolutely tell me if I looked weird—if she swears up and down that I look totally fine, I do have this momentary thought of, 'Well, she wouldn't lie to me.' So I try to hold onto that. I really try. I'll sit there and think, 'Okay, maybe my brain is just playing tricks on me, maybe I'm just tired.' 

But it just... it evaporates. It completely evaporates the second I catch my reflection again. Like just yesterday, I was getting into my car, and I glanced in the rearview mirror just to check behind me, not even trying to look at myself, and boom. There it was. The left side just looked so heavy and distorted compared to the right, just puffy and hanging there. 

So, no matter how much I try to reason with myself, or how much logic I try to apply—and I really do try to be logical about this, I'll literally list out the reasons in my head why my perception might be skewed—it just doesn't matter. The visual evidence is just too strong for me. It feels absolutely, one hundred percent certain. It's like... it's like if someone told you the sky was green, but you're looking right at it and it's clearly blue. You might question yourself for a split second if every single person around you is screaming that it's green, but your own eyes are telling you it's blue. That's exactly how it feels with my cheek and my jaw. I just can't shake it. Even when I minimize my video window during those support calls, thinking maybe if I don't look at it I'll realize it's all in my head, the certainty is just always there, humming in the background. I just know it's swollen, and I can't un-know it, no matter how much I want to.
Would you say that your concern about the left side of your face being swollen is excessive, or do you believe it is a realistic and accurate perception of how you actually look?

I mean... it’s kind of a two-part thing, I guess? Like, if you're asking if the amount of time I spend worrying about it is excessive... then yes, absolutely. I mean, that’s literally why I came in to see you today. I just... I can't stop focusing on how uneven and puffy the left side of my face looks. It’s taking up so much space in my brain, it's exhausting. 

Like I was saying before, whether I'm on those endless video calls for work, trying to troubleshoot some guy's VPN while staring at my own little square, or I'm looking at those salsa photos from the weekend... it’s just all I can see. I'll zoom in, I'll analyze the shadows, I'll compare it to older photos... it's a whole process. And it really is starting to mess with my work and my social life, to the point where I'm literally hiding from my webcam and avoiding dance nights altogether just so I don't have to deal with the photographic evidence. So, the preoccupation part? The fact that it's ruining my schedule? Definitely excessive. 

But... if you're asking if I think the swelling *itself* is just in my head? No. I believe what I'm seeing is a completely realistic and accurate perception of how I actually look. I know everyone keeps telling me they don't see anything, and my friends think I'm being ridiculous for even bringing it up, but... I know what I'm looking at. The camera doesn't lie, you know? The webcam at my desk, the iPhones at the dance socials... they capture exactly what's there. The lens doesn't have a bias. So, I know the puffiness is real, and I know it's incredibly obvious. I just... I wish I could be one of those people who has a glaring physical flaw and just doesn't care, but instead, I'm letting it dictate my entire life.

Do you find yourself performing any specific behaviors or mental rituals—like checking mirrors, taking certain angles in photos, or comparing your face to others—whenever you feel anxious about the left side of your face?

Oh, gosh... yes. So much yes. It's honestly become this whole exhausting ordeal that I can't seem to stop doing. 

Like, before I even join a meeting for work—and I do a lot of remote support, so I'm on camera constantly—I will spend I don't even know how long just opening and closing the camera preview on my monitor. I'll pull up the little video settings window, and I'll just sit there staring at myself, trying to figure out how bad the swelling looks that day. And then I start messing with everything. I'll move my desk lamp around to change the lighting, trying to wash out the shadow on my left cheek. I'll adjust my chair height, I'll tilt my webcam up, then down, then slightly to the right, just desperately trying to find an angle where my face doesn't look completely lopsided. 

And my hair... oh my god, the amount of time I spend on my hair. I have this whole routine where I try to sweep it over the left side of my jaw to hide the puffiness. But then I'll look in the preview and think, 'No, that looks too obvious, people are going to know I'm hiding something.' So I'll redo it. I'll pull different pieces down, tuck others behind my ear, use bobby pins, take them out... just endlessly fixing and refixing my hair around that side of my face until my scalp literally hurts. 

It's even worse if I'm actually trying to go out somewhere in person. Like if I'm supposed to go to a salsa night with my friends, I will stand in front of my mirror and take maybe fifty or sixty pictures on my phone. Just retaking and retaking them, analyzing every single one to see if the swelling is noticeable. And then the interrogations start. I will text my friends the pictures, or if they're picking me up, I'll just barrage them with questions. 'Does this look weird? Can you tell my cheek is swollen today? Be honest, do I look strange? Is it really obvious?' And they always say no, they always sigh and tell me I look fine, but I just can't let it go. I'll keep asking them, trying to read their faces to see if they're just lying to make me feel better. 

And the worst part is, I do this for so long that I end up making myself incredibly late for whatever it is I'm supposed to be doing. Or... honestly, half the time, by the time I've gone through all the camera checks and the lighting adjustments and the hair fixing and interrogating my friends... I'm just done. I am so emotionally and physically drained from the anxiety of it all that I just cancel. I'll just sit on my bed, completely exhausted, and I won't even go. I just don't have the energy left to face people when I feel like I look like that.
Have you ever thought that maybe everyone else is lying to you or just refusing to acknowledge that your left cheek looks swollen, even though you can see it so clearly?

I mean... I wouldn't say I think they're *lying* lying. Not like some big, organized conspiracy where everyone I know has had a secret meeting to agree to gaslight me about my face. I don't think that at all. It's not malicious. I just... I think it's more about how human beings are wired to interact, you know? 

Like, if you really think about it, when someone asks you, 'Hey, does my face look weird today?' the automatic, knee-jerk social response is almost always going to be, 'No, of course not, you look totally fine!' It's just the script we all follow. Like when my friend Sarah—the one from grad school I was talking about earlier—when she asks me if a certain outfit makes her look bad, my first instinct is always to reassure her, even if it's maybe not the most flattering cut on her. You just want to make the people you care about feel good. So I really feel like that's what my friends and family are doing with me. They see how incredibly stressed and anxious I am about my cheek, they see me taking fifty photos in the mirror and completely freaking out, and they just want to calm me down. They're trying to be good friends by saying, 'I don't see it, you look great, don't worry.' They're just trying to spare my feelings.

And the other piece of it is... I just don't think anyone else is examining me under a microscope the way I am. Like, when I'm doing remote support for work, the person on the other end of the screen is stressed about their own stuff. They just want their email to work or their network drive to connect. They aren't staring at my little video square, analyzing the volume of my left jawline compared to my right. And even my friends, when we're at a salsa night or something, they're looking at the whole room, or they're looking at their own phones, or worrying about their own dancing. They haven't spent the last two hours adjusting a desk lamp and staring at a webcam preview like I have. 

So when I ask them if I look swollen, they probably just do a quick, half-second glance and say they don't see anything because they literally haven't studied it. So, no, I don't think they're refusing to acknowledge it out of spite or actively lying to trick me. I just think they aren't looking closely enough to see it, or they're just defaulting to being polite. But I'm the one who has to actually live in this face and see the reality of it every single day, so I can't just brush it off the way they do.

Have you ever had any experiences where you believed something strongly that others didn't, even when they gave you clear evidence that it wasn't true—something other than your concern about your face?

No... no, I don't think so. Like, if you're asking if I have some sort of... I don't know, wild conspiracy theories or if I think people are following me or something? Definitely not. I'm actually a very logical person. I mean, I have a graduate degree, I work as a computer support specialist... my entire day is literally just looking at evidence, you know? 

Like, if a user tells me their system is totally broken and they're panicking, but I look at the error logs and the network diagnostics and the hard data, and it shows me it's just a disconnected VPN or a wrong password, I believe the data. I don't just make up a reality that isn't there. I rely on facts. If someone gives me clear proof of something in my day-to-day life, I accept it. I'm very grounded in that way. I don't have any weird beliefs about the world or other people or anything like that. 

It really is just... just this one thing. And honestly, I think that's part of why this whole situation with my face is so incredibly frustrating to me. Because I *know* I'm a rational person. I know how to analyze a problem and look at the facts. I pay my bills, I manage complex IT issues, I can read a room. But when it comes to my left cheek, the facts are right there on the screen. The webcam is the data, you know? The photos are the proof. I'm looking right at the evidence of the puffiness. So it feels completely different to me than just, like, making something up in my head despite what people say. But outside of that? No, absolutely nothing else. Just the swelling.
Is your main concern about the left side of your face being swollen specifically about how it looks, or is it more about a need for things to feel even or just right?

Oh, it's definitely about how it looks. It's not... I don't have some sort of internal sensation where my face physically feels off-balance or weird, you know? It's not a sensory thing where I just need to touch it to make it feel right. It is entirely, one hundred percent visual. It's the appearance of it. 

Actually, that's the whole reason I finally made this appointment and came in to see you. Because I just... I can't stop focusing on how uneven and puffy the left side of my face looks. It's like I'm trapped staring at it. Especially on those video calls for work, or when I'm swiping through those photos from salsa night that I was telling you about. I look at the screen and the puffiness is just glaring at me. It's all I can see. And it's so incredibly frustrating because, like I said, everyone keeps telling me they don't see anything. They look at the exact same photo and tell me my face is totally normal, but I'm looking right at the unevenness! 

So it's not that I need things to just "feel right" in some abstract way. I don't care about perfect symmetry in my apartment or my IT closet at work or anything like that. It's specifically that my face looks swollen to me, and it's starting to completely mess with my work and my social life. The fact that I'm obsessing over how bad it looks on camera is why I'm making myself late for my support tickets, and why I'm canceling on my friends. The appearance of it is just ruining everything for me right now.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms along with the swelling you see, like pain, numbness, or difficulty moving that side of your face?

No, no, nothing like that at all. It doesn't hurt, it's not numb... I can move it perfectly fine. Like, I can smile, I can talk, I can chew my food without any issues whatsoever. 

Actually, that's something I've checked a lot, because obviously when you see swelling, your first logical thought is usually, 'Oh, is it a tooth infection? Did I get bitten by a spider in my sleep? Is it an allergy?' So I'll sit there in front of my webcam—usually when I'm supposed to be logging in to check the ticketing queue for the morning—and I'll just, like, stretch my mouth, puff out my cheeks, move my jaw side to side, just to see if there's any stiffness or if it catches or hurts when I do certain expressions. And there's nothing. It feels exactly like the right side of my face. If I just close my eyes and sit perfectly still, I wouldn't even know anything was wrong. It's only when I open my eyes and look at the monitor or the mirror that I see the puffiness. 

I've even poked at it, you know, just pressing around the jawline and up by the cheekbone to see if it's tender, because sometimes if you have a swollen lymph node or a sinus thing, it aches when you press on it. But it doesn't ache at all. There's zero pain, no tingling, no weird nerve sensations, and I can move every muscle just fine. It's just... it just looks so puffy and uneven. Which honestly almost makes it more maddening, you know? Because if it hurt, at least I'd have a physical symptom to take to a regular medical doctor and say, 'Hey, this side of my face is throbbing, please fix it.' But because it just *looks* like this and feels completely normal, I'm just stuck staring at it.

inference_history.note: The patient presents with persistent preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance (asymmetry and puffiness of the left side of the face), causing significant distress and impairment in social and occupational functioning. The preoccupation is not fully aligned with typical obsessive-compulsive themes, making F42.2 (Body Dysmorphic Disorder) the leading candidate. Other differential diagnoses include F45.22 (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder), F21 (Delusional Disorder, somatic type), and F45.8 (Other specified neurotic disorders) as less likely possibilities depending on further clarification.

The patient's preoccupation with a perceived facial defect (left side of face appearing swollen and uneven) that persists despite reassurance from others and their detailed description of repetitive behaviors (e.g., checking in mirrors, adjusting camera angles, analyzing their face in photos) strongly support Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22). The persistence of the belief, despite moments of doubt, and the degree of insight being variable but overridden by perceptual conviction, makes F45.22 the most likely diagnosis. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (F42.2) remains a candidate due to the obsessive nature of the thoughts and repetitive behaviors, but the content is more consistent with a body image disturbance. Schizophrenia spectrum (F21) is unlikely given no evidence of delusions independent of appearance concerns or other psychotic features. Other neurotic disorders (F45.8) are ruled out due to the specificity of the concern.

I'll move my desk lamp around to change the lighting, trying to wash out the shadow on my left cheek. I'll adjust my chair height, I'll tilt my webcam up, then down, then slightly to the right, just desperately trying to find an angle where my face doesn't look completely lopsided. 

And my hair... oh my god, the amount of time I spend on my hair. I have this whole routine where I try to sweep it over the left side of my jaw to hide the puffiness. But then I'll look in the preview and think, 'No, that looks too obvious, people are going to know I'm hiding something.' So I'll redo it. I'll pull different pieces down, tuck others behind my ear, use bobby pins, take them out... just endlessly fixing and refixing my hair around that side of my face until my scalp literally hurts. 

It's even worse if I'm actually trying to go out somewhere in person. Like if I'm supposed to go to a salsa night with my friends, I will stand in front of my mirror and take maybe fifty or sixty pictures on my phone. Just retaking and retaking them, analyzing every single one to see if the swelling is noticeable. And then the interrogations start. I will text my friends the pictures, or if they're picking me up, I'll just barrage them with questions. 'Does this look weird? Can you tell my cheek is swollen today? Be honest, do I look strange? Is it really obvious?' And they always say no, they always sigh and tell me I look fine, but I just can't let it go. I'll keep asking them, trying to read their faces to see if they're just lying to make me feel better. 

And the worst part is, I do this for so long that I end up making myself incredibly late for whatever it is I'm supposed to be doing. Or... honestly, half the time, by the time I've gone through all the camera checks and the lighting adjustments and the hair fixing and interrogating my friends... I'm just done. I am so emotionally and physically drained from the anxiety of it all that I just cancel. I'll just sit on my bed, completely exhausted, and I won't even go. I just don't have the energy left to face people when I feel like I look like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's preoccupation with the perceived facial asymmetry meets the threshold for a delusional belief, which would support the diagnosis of delusional disorder (F22.0) rather than body dysmorphic disorder (F45.22).
doctor.question: Have you ever thought that maybe everyone else is lying to you or just refusing to acknowledge that your left cheek looks swollen, even though you can see it so clearly?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about delusional beliefs or paranoia regarding others lying about the perceived defect, which relates to the level of insight. This is not covered by the provided symptom profile items (Preoccupation with Appearance, Appearance-Related Repetitive Behaviors, or Functional Impairment).

patient.answer:
I mean... I wouldn't say I think they're *lying* lying. Not like some big, organized conspiracy where everyone I know has had a secret meeting to agree to gaslight me about my face. I don't think that at all. It's not malicious. I just... I think it's more about how human beings are wired to interact, you know? 

Like, if you really think about it, when someone asks you, 'Hey, does my face look weird today?' the automatic, knee-jerk social response is almost always going to be, 'No, of course not, you look totally fine!' It's just the script we all follow. Like when my friend Sarah—the one from grad school I was talking about earlier—when she asks me if a certain outfit makes her look bad, my first instinct is always to reassure her, even if it's maybe not the most flattering cut on her. You just want to make the people you care about feel good. So I really feel like that's what my friends and family are doing with me. They see how incredibly stressed and anxious I am about my cheek, they see me taking fifty photos in the mirror and completely freaking out, and they just want to calm me down. They're trying to be good friends by saying, 'I don't see it, you look great, don't worry.' They're just trying to spare my feelings.

And the other piece of it is... I just don't think anyone else is examining me under a microscope the way I am. Like, when I'm doing remote support for work, the person on the other end of the screen is stressed about their own stuff. They just want their email to work or their network drive to connect. They aren't staring at my little video square, analyzing the volume of my left jawline compared to my right. And even my friends, when we're at a salsa night or something, they're looking at the whole room, or they're looking at their own phones, or worrying about their own dancing. They haven't spent the last two hours adjusting a desk lamp and staring at a webcam preview like I have. 

So when I ask them if I look swollen, they probably just do a quick, half-second glance and say they don't see anything because they literally haven't studied it. So, no, I don't think they're refusing to acknowledge it out of spite or actively lying to trick me. I just think they aren't looking closely enough to see it, or they're just defaulting to being polite. But I'm the one who has to actually live in this face and see the reality of it every single day, so I can't just brush it off the way they do.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has any history of delusional beliefs or fixed false beliefs that are not limited to concerns about appearance, which would support a delusional disorder specifier rather than a body dysmorphic disorder diagnosis.
doctor.question: Have you ever had any experiences where you believed something strongly that others didn't, even when they gave you clear evidence that it wasn't true—something other than your concern about your face?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about delusional beliefs unrelated to the appearance concern, which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No... no, I don't think so. Like, if you're asking if I have some sort of... I don't know, wild conspiracy theories or if I think people are following me or something? Definitely not. I'm actually a very logical person. I mean, I have a graduate degree, I work as a computer support specialist... my entire day is literally just looking at evidence, you know? 

Like, if a user tells me their system is totally broken and they're panicking, but I look at the error logs and the network diagnostics and the hard data, and it shows me it's just a disconnected VPN or a wrong password, I believe the data. I don't just make up a reality that isn't there. I rely on facts. If someone gives me clear proof of something in my day-to-day life, I accept it. I'm very grounded in that way. I don't have any weird beliefs about the world or other people or anything like that. 

It really is just... just this one thing. And honestly, I think that's part of why this whole situation with my face is so incredibly frustrating to me. Because I *know* I'm a rational person. I know how to analyze a problem and look at the facts. I pay my bills, I manage complex IT issues, I can read a room. But when it comes to my left cheek, the facts are right there on the screen. The webcam is the data, you know? The photos are the proof. I'm looking right at the evidence of the puffiness. So it feels completely different to me than just, like, making something up in my head despite what people say. But outside of that? No, absolutely nothing else. Just the swelling.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concern is better explained by body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) or obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), based on whether the preoccupation is primarily with a perceived defect in appearance (BDD) versus intrusive thoughts or compulsions related to symmetry or order (OCD).
doctor.question: Is your main concern about the left side of your face being swollen specifically about how it looks, or is it more about a need for things to feel even or just right?

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can't stop focusing on how uneven and puffy the left side of my face looks on video calls and in salsa photos, even though everyone keeps telling me they don't see anything, and it's starting to mess with my work and social life.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking to clarify the nature of my concern about my face—whether it's driven by distress over its physical appearance (perceived flaw/defect) or a different issue like a 'just right' OCD feeling. This maps directly to the preoccupation with appearance symptom.

patient.answer:
Oh, it's definitely about how it looks. It's not... I don't have some sort of internal sensation where my face physically feels off-balance or weird, you know? It's not a sensory thing where I just need to touch it to make it feel right. It is entirely, one hundred percent visual. It's the appearance of it. 

Actually, that's the whole reason I finally made this appointment and came in to see you. Because I just... I can't stop focusing on how uneven and puffy the left side of my face looks. It's like I'm trapped staring at it. Especially on those video calls for work, or when I'm swiping through those photos from salsa night that I was telling you about. I look at the screen and the puffiness is just glaring at me. It's all I can see. And it's so incredibly frustrating because, like I said, everyone keeps telling me they don't see anything. They look at the exact same photo and tell me my face is totally normal, but I'm looking right at the unevenness! 

So it's not that I need things to just "feel right" in some abstract way. I don't care about perfect symmetry in my apartment or my IT closet at work or anything like that. It's specifically that my face looks swollen to me, and it's starting to completely mess with my work and my social life. The fact that I'm obsessing over how bad it looks on camera is why I'm making myself late for my support tickets, and why I'm canceling on my friends. The appearance of it is just ruining everything for me right now.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences any additional physical symptoms or concerns related to the perceived facial swelling, which could indicate a somatic focus or contribute to the differential diagnosis.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any physical symptoms along with the swelling you see, like pain, numbness, or difficulty moving that side of your face?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical or neurological symptoms (pain, numbness, difficulty moving) to rule out a medical condition, which is not covered by the patient's Body Dysmorphic Disorder symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no, nothing like that at all. It doesn't hurt, it's not numb... I can move it perfectly fine. Like, I can smile, I can talk, I can chew my food without any issues whatsoever. 

Actually, that's something I've checked a lot, because obviously when you see swelling, your first logical thought is usually, 'Oh, is it a tooth infection? Did I get bitten by a spider in my sleep? Is it an allergy?' So I'll sit there in front of my webcam—usually when I'm supposed to be logging in to check the ticketing queue for the morning—and I'll just, like, stretch my mouth, puff out my cheeks, move my jaw side to side, just to see if there's any stiffness or if it catches or hurts when I do certain expressions. And there's nothing. It feels exactly like the right side of my face. If I just close my eyes and sit perfectly still, I wouldn't even know anything was wrong. It's only when I open my eyes and look at the monitor or the mirror that I see the puffiness. 

I've even poked at it, you know, just pressing around the jawline and up by the cheekbone to see if it's tender, because sometimes if you have a swollen lymph node or a sinus thing, it aches when you press on it. But it doesn't ache at all. There's zero pain, no tingling, no weird nerve sensations, and I can move every muscle just fine. It's just... it just looks so puffy and uneven. Which honestly almost makes it more maddening, you know? Because if it hurt, at least I'd have a physical symptom to take to a regular medical doctor and say, 'Hey, this side of my face is throbbing, please fix it.' But because it just *looks* like this and feels completely normal, I'm just stuck staring at it.

opening_question.intent: Establish the patient's primary concern or reason for seeking help
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a primary preoccupation with a perceived defect in physical appearance (left side of the face appears uneven and swollen) that is not observable to others. The belief is associated with significant distress and impairment in social and occupational functioning. The patient acknowledges the preoccupation is excessive, engages in repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, lighting adjustment, photo analysis), and the concern is exclusively appearance-related, not driven by a need for symmetry or order. The belief, while held with strong conviction, is not completely fixed or delusional in nature, as the patient shows some capacity for reality testing, distinguishing this from a delusional disorder.
